title: Jump statements
hook: `break`, `continue`, `return`, and `goto` move the instruction pointer. In production code you will use the first three constantly and `goto` almost never — except `goto case` in a classic switch.

sections.heading: break, continue, return, goto
sections.prose: `break` leaves the innermost `switch`, loop, or (rarely) labeled statement. `continue` skips to the next loop iteration. `return` exits the method (or top-level program) and optionally yields a value. `goto label;` jumps to a label in the same method; `goto case 2;` / `goto default;` are the supported switch fall-through. Do not use `goto` to skip `finally` cleanup — you cannot jump out of a `finally` anyway, and dispose belongs in `using` (module 06). In an SQS batch loop, `continue` on a poison payload after logging is clearer than nested ifs.

snippets.label: continue on bad messages; return a code
snippets.explanation: Stacked `case 1: case 2:` without code between is not fall-through of statements; it is multiple labels on one section. Statement fall-through still needs `goto case`.

interviewTakeaways: `break`/`continue` affect the nearest loop or switch.
`return` from Main/top-level sets the process exit code when the type is `int`.
`goto` is legal; cite `goto case` if asked for a legitimate use.
commonPitfalls: Using `goto` across try/finally and fighting the compiler.
Returning from a `void` lambda by habit of JS `return` in `forEach` — different construct (delegates later).

jsTsCorrelations.note: Same words, same idea. JS labeled statements exist but are rare; C# labels are mainly for goto. JS switch fall-through is the default; C# forbids it without goto case.
